title: Mock paper 2
intro:
**120 minutes · 100 marks.** Same structure as the final paper, with more semaphores, concurrent data structures, patterns and deadlock theory:

| Section | Marks | What |
|---|---|---|
| A - MCQ | 50 | 3 scenarios × 5 questions, then 10 theory questions (2 marks each) |
| B - Code-based | 40 | 8 questions × 5: fill the gaps, arrange the lines, spot the bug |
| C - Full code | 10 | One complete program, self-marked against a rubric |

Fill-the-gap and arrange questions earn partial credit; MCQs and spot-the-line are all or nothing.

sections.title: Section A - MCQ
sections.blurb: Each scenario describes a program and what was observed when it ran; five questions follow it. Questions 16–25 are on the theory. 2 marks each, one answer is correct.

scenarios.title: Scenario 1 · Car-park ramp
Scenario 2 · Inventory service
scenarios.text:
An inventory service keeps product ids in a **sorted linked list** shared by many threads (insert, delete, contains), and a shared **stock counter**. Two list versions exist: one global mutex for the whole list (coarse-grained), and one mutex per node with hand-over-hand locking (fine-grained). Three counter versions exist: a mutex around `stock++`, a compare-and-swap retry loop, and `__sync_fetch_and_add`.

Benchmarks on a **2-core** laptop, `gcc -O2`:

| Benchmark (8 threads) | Result |
|---|---|
| List, coarse-grained | 1.5 M ops/s |
| List, fine-grained | 0.09 M ops/s |
| Counter, mutex | 0.59 s, correct |
| Counter, CAS loop | 0.40 s, correct |
| Counter, fetch-and-add | 0.17 s, correct |
| Counter, no synchronisation | correct total, ~0 s |

scenarios.title: Scenario 3 · Log-processing pipeline
scenarios.text:
A log processor runs three stages connected by bounded queues: **read** a record (1 ms), **parse** it (6 ms), **write** the result (1 ms). Each stage runs in its own thread on a 4-core machine. At the end, the reader sends one *poison pill* into the read→parse queue; a parse thread that receives the pill forwards it to the write stage and exits.

A second tool processes 200 independent *reports* whose costs differ by up to 100×. Version P uses a thread pool where each worker grabs the next report index from a shared counter. Version W gives each worker its own double-ended queue and lets idle workers steal from others.

questions.prompt: What does the semaphore `cap` (initial value 4) implement?
options: A multiplex: at most 4 threads can be past `sem_wait(&cap)` at the same time
questions.explain: A counting semaphore initialised to N admits N threads before the next one blocks.

questions.prompt: The first car up waits on `ramp` while still holding `mutex_up`. Is that a deadlock risk?
options: No: later up cars simply queue on `mutex_up` behind it, and the down side releases `ramp` without needing `mutex_up`, so no cycle can form
Yes: a semaphore must never be waited on while another is held
Yes: the last car down needs `mutex_up` to post `ramp`
questions.explain: This is the lightswitch pattern. Holding a lock while blocking is only dangerous if the thread that would wake you needs that same lock.

questions.prompt: A developer removes the `mutex_up` waits and posts "for speed". What can go wrong?
options: Only the speed changes: more than 4 cars can now be on the ramp
Updates of `n_up` race, so two cars can both act as "first" (or "last"), and `ramp` is taken or released the wrong number of times - opposite traffic on the ramp, or a ramp never released
questions.explain: The count and the decision based on it must be one critical section.

questions.prompt: At peak time cars keep arriving to go up. What happens to cars waiting to go down, and what is the standard fix?
options: They can wait indefinitely because `n_up` never returns to 0 (starvation); add a turnstile semaphore every car passes on arrival, which a waiting down car holds
The system deadlocks; reorder the semaphores
They enter as soon as 4 cars are on the ramp
questions.explain: The lightswitch gives the active direction priority, exactly like readers in a reader-preference readers–writers lock.

questions.prompt: Why does the colleague's barrier (one counter, one semaphore) fail when used for several rounds?
options: Semaphores cannot block more than 4 threads
A fast attendant can pass, start the next round and arrive at the barrier again before slow ones have left it, taking a token meant for them
A semaphore can be posted only once
questions.explain: A reusable barrier needs two phases (two turnstiles) so nobody re-enters until everyone has left.

questions.prompt: Why is the fine-grained list about 16 times slower than the coarse-grained one here?
options: Every step of every traversal locks and unlocks a node, and all operations start at the head lock, so threads form a convoy - with only 2 cores there is no parallelism to win back the overhead
Fine-grained locking always deadlocks under load
The coarse list skips locking for `contains`
Fine-grained lists cannot be compiled with `-O2`
questions.explain: Fine-grained locking pays off with many cores, long lists and operations spread over the structure.

questions.prompt: In the fine-grained list a thread unlocks `pred` before locking `curr`. What can go wrong?
options: The list becomes unsorted only if keys are equal
In the gap another thread can delete `curr` or insert between `pred` and `curr`, so the thread follows a freed pointer or links into a node no longer in the list
questions.explain: Hold the previous lock until the next one is acquired; that keeps the pair stable.

questions.prompt: Which classification of the three correct counters is right?
options: Mutex - blocking; CAS loop - wait-free; fetch-and-add - lock-free
Mutex - lock-free; CAS loop - wait-free; fetch-and-add - blocking
Mutex - blocking; CAS loop - lock-free; fetch-and-add - wait-free
questions.explain: A delayed lock holder blocks everyone; a CAS loop always lets someone succeed but may starve one thread; fetch-and-add finishes in bounded steps.

questions.prompt: Why is fetch-and-add (0.17 s) faster than the CAS loop (0.40 s) under contention?
options: Fetch-and-add is executed by the compiler at build time
CAS cannot be used on `long` variables
Fetch-and-add always succeeds in one atomic instruction; most CAS attempts fail and must re-read and retry, each costing another cache-line transfer
questions.explain: Both are lock-free primitives, but failed CAS attempts are wasted work.

questions.prompt: The unsynchronised counter gives the correct total at `-O2`. What should you conclude?
options: The counter is correct at `-O2` and needs no synchronisation
The race still exists; the compiler folded the loop into one addition per thread, shrinking the window so collisions are rare
Two cores cannot produce a race
questions.explain: A test passing is not proof. Rebuild at `-O0` or make the variable `volatile` and the lost updates return.

questions.prompt: With one thread per stage, what is the steady-state throughput?
options: About 167 records per second - one per 6 ms, set by the parse stage
About 125 records per second (one per 8 ms)
questions.explain: A pipeline runs at the pace of its slowest stage; latency per record is still 8 ms.

questions.prompt: Two more parse threads are added (three in total). What throughput should you expect?
options: About 500 records per second - parsing now delivers one record every 2 ms, and the 1 ms stages are not yet the bottleneck
questions.explain: Throughput = 1 / max(stage time / workers) = 1 / max(1, 6/3, 1) ms.

questions.prompt: With three parse threads the program now hangs at exit. Why?
options: The write stage exits too early
Poison pills cannot pass through bounded queues
The bounded queues are too small
Only one poison pill is sent, so one parse thread exits and the other two block for ever on the empty queue
questions.explain: Send one pill per consumer of a queue (and have the write stage wait for one pill per parse thread).

questions.prompt: Why does version P balance the uneven reports well compared with giving each worker a fixed block of 200/n reports?
options: Version P sorts the reports by cost first
Version P runs reports in parallel inside each worker
Workers take the next report when they finish one, so a worker that drew an expensive report simply takes fewer; with fixed blocks, whoever owns several expensive reports finishes last
Fixed blocks have a race condition
questions.explain: Dynamic task assignment trades one tiny critical section (or atomic increment) per task for balance.

questions.prompt: In version W a worker pops from the back of its own deque but steals from the front of another's. Why?
options: The front of a deque is always empty
The owner gets its newest, cache-hot task; a thief takes the oldest (usually largest) task from the other end, so owner and thief rarely contend
Stealing from the back is impossible with a mutex
questions.explain: LIFO locally for locality, FIFO for steals for big chunks and low contention.

questions.prompt: In the Banker's algorithm, a request passes Request ≤ Need and Request ≤ Available, but the pretend-grant state is unsafe. What happens?
options: The request is not granted; the process waits and the state is rolled back
It is granted, because unsafe is not deadlocked
The OS pre-empts resources from another process
questions.explain: Unsafe means deadlock can no longer be ruled out, so the OS keeps the system in a safe state.

questions.prompt: A resource-allocation graph with only single-instance resources contains a cycle. What can you conclude?
options: The system is in a safe state
The processes in the cycle are deadlocked
Deadlock is possible but not certain
There is no deadlock unless the graph is also disconnected
questions.explain: With one instance per resource a cycle is necessary and sufficient. With several instances it is only necessary.

questions.prompt: The Filter lock generalises Peterson's algorithm to n threads. Which property does it lose?
questions.explain: A thread can be overtaken many times while climbing the levels. The Bakery lock restores FCFS with tickets.

questions.prompt: In CUDA, which statement about `__syncthreads()` is correct?
options: It copies data from the host to the device
It is a barrier for the threads of one block only; there is no barrier across blocks inside a kernel
It synchronises every thread in the grid
questions.explain: Blocks may not even be resident at the same time; grid-wide synchronisation needs a kernel boundary.

questions.prompt: Two ranks each call `MPI_Send` of a large message to the other and then `MPI_Recv`. What can happen?
options: It always works because MPI buffers every message
The messages are delivered out of order
Deadlock: each send may block until the matching receive is posted, which never happens
questions.explain: Small messages are often buffered, so the bug only appears for large ones. Order the calls, or use `MPI_Sendrecv` / non-blocking calls.

questions.prompt: Which collective leaves the combined result (for example a sum) on every rank?
questions.explain: `MPI_Reduce` leaves it on the root only; `Allreduce` = reduce + broadcast.

questions.prompt: A recursive sum spawns a new thread for every subtree with more than 100 nodes. It runs 100× slower than the serial version. Why?
options: The tree is unbalanced, so threads deadlock
Creating and joining a thread costs microseconds while summing 100 nodes costs nanoseconds, so tens of thousands of threads are pure overhead
questions.explain: Each task must do much more work than it costs to create; raise the threshold to a few large tasks per core.

questions.prompt: Which statement matches Gustafson's view of speedup?
options: Adding processors always reduces efficiency to zero
Speedup can never exceed 1/(1 − p) for any problem size
Speedup is limited by the span
If the problem size grows with the number of processors, the serial fraction shrinks in relative terms and speedup can grow almost linearly
questions.explain: Amdahl fixes the problem size (strong scaling); Gustafson grows it (weak scaling): $S = (1 - p) + pn$.

questions.prompt: Why can a combiner not simply apply the reduce function for computing an average?
options: Averages cannot be computed with MapReduce
The average of partial averages is not the overall average; emit (sum, count) pairs and divide in the reducer
Combiners run on the reducer machine
questions.explain: A combiner is safe for associative and commutative operations such as sum, max, min and count.

questions.prompt: In a lock-free stack, a thread reads top = A, is delayed, and meanwhile others pop A, pop B and push A back. Its CAS(top, A, next) succeeds and corrupts the stack. What is this called?
questions.explain: The pointer value matches but the structure changed. Fix with a version counter beside the pointer, hazard pointers, or safe memory reclamation.

sections.title: Section B - Code-based
sections.blurb: 8 questions, 5 marks each. Choose the missing lines, drag the lines into order (or use the arrows), or click the faulty line(s).

questions.prompt: Arrange the semaphore-based **producer** of a bounded buffer (`spaces` = N, `items` = 0, `mutex` = 1).
questions.explain: Reserve a slot first, then lock the buffer, write, unlock, and announce an item. Swapping the two waits deadlocks on a full buffer.

questions.prompt: Complete the bridge **lightswitch** for direction `d` (first car locks the bridge, last car releases it).
questions.explain: The first car in (count becomes 1) claims the bridge; the last out (count becomes 0) releases it. The capacity semaphore (init 3) is the multiplex.

questions.prompt: This reader-preference `start_read`/`end_read` pair has bugs. Click every faulty line.
questions.explain: Line 3 must be `while` (spurious wakeups / barging). Line 11 must test `reader_count == 0` - the *last* reader out wakes a writer.

questions.prompt: Complete the OpenMP task-parallel merge sort launch and recursion.
questions.explain: Both halves become tasks; `taskwait` waits for the two children before merging (a `barrier` inside a task is illegal). `single` makes one thread start the recursion.

questions.prompt: Work-stealing deque: the owner pops from the back, thieves steal from the front. Click the faulty line.
questions.explain: A thief must take from the front: `t = d->items[d->front++];`. Line 11 makes thieves pop the owner’s end, so they contend with the owner and grab small, cache-hot tasks.

questions.prompt: Arrange the middle-stage thread of a three-stage pipeline (dequeue, process, forward; on the poison pill, pass it on to the last stage and stop).
questions.explain: Stage 1 sends one pill per stage-2 worker; each worker forwards its pill to stage 3 and exits, and stage 3 stops after it has counted one pill per stage-2 worker. Processing before checking for the pill would push garbage downstream.

questions.prompt: Complete the wait-free and lock-free increments.
questions.explain: FAA is a single always-succeeding atomic. In the CAS loop, read `counter` into `old`, then swap only if `counter` still equals `old`.

questions.prompt: This OpenMP Monte Carlo π code gives a wrong (and varying) answer with 4 threads. Click the line that causes it.
questions.explain: `count` is shared and `count++` races. Add `reduction(+:count)` to the pragma, or `#pragma omp atomic` before the increment.

sections.title: Section C - Full code
sections.blurb: One complete program, 10 marks. After you submit, the model solution and a rubric appear - tick what you achieved.

questions.prompt:
Write a complete C program that uses **POSIX semaphores only** (no condition variables) for a bounded buffer of size 10 shared by **P producers and C consumers** (P, C and K from `argv`).

- Producer `p` puts `p*1000 + j` for `j = 0 … K−1`.
- Each consumer takes items until it receives a sentinel `-1`; `main` must arrange exactly **C** sentinels after all producers finish.
- Count the items consumed (protect the counter) and print `produced=… consumed=… MATCH` (or `MISMATCH`).

rubric.text: `put`/`get` wait on the counting semaphore **before** the mutex, and post the opposite counter after unlocking
Circular indices updated inside the mutex
Producers generate `p*1000 + j`; ids passed safely (by value or a per-thread slot)
Exactly C sentinels, put only after all producers are joined; every consumer stops on one
Consumed count protected (semaphore/mutex or atomic) and compared with P × K
All threads created and joined; semaphores destroyed

questions.explain: Tick each rubric item your program fully satisfies. The classic mistakes: waiting on `mutex` before `spaces` (deadlock on a full buffer), one sentinel for several consumers (hang at the end), or passing `&i` as the producer id.
